Linguistic Typology. The classification of languages by their recurrent structural features—how they form words, arrange them, organize meaning, and handle grammatical information. Typologists ask questions like: Does this language use prefixes, suffixes, or infixes? Does it express tense before the verb or after? Is its baseline word order subject-verb-object or subject-object-verb? By mapping such features across the world's languages, linguists identify universal patterns, rare structures, and the boundaries of human linguistic possibility.

The foundational distinction is morphological type. Isolating languages like Chinese and English use few inflections and rely on word order. Agglutinative languages like Turkish and Basque stack morphemes linearly and transparently. Fusional languages like Latin and Russian combine multiple grammatical meanings into single morphemes. Polysynthetic languages like Navajo and Inuit encode entire clauses within single words. Word order typology reveals correlations. Languages with verb-initial order often use postpositions and possess other rare features together, as if core grammatical decisions cascade through the system.

Basque is a typological outlier—an agglutinative language with ergative-absolutive alignment and postpositions, surviving in a region surrounded by Indo-European accusative-nominative languages. Hungarian exemplifies agglutinative structure and postpositional alignment. Its vowel harmony and extensive case system make it a standard textbook example of an agglutinative language. Navajo is the canonical example of a polysynthetic language. Its verb system encodes subject, object, aspect, mood, and direction within a single word, allowing complete thoughts in a single word.

Language universals emerge from typology. All languages have nouns and verbs. All languages express negation. All languages can form questions. These universals suggest deep constraints on human language. Typological research has practical value. Understanding grammatical features aids language documentation, second-language teaching, and machine translation. It also constrains theories of human cognition and universal grammar. Linguistics is the broader science of language where typology is one major subfield. Noam Chomsky's universal grammar theory overlaps with typology. Chomsky asks what features are universal versus parametric. Structural linguistics is how typology emerged from structuralist approaches to systematic comparison across languages. Basque is a crucial typological outlier exhibiting rare combinations of features. Hungarian is a standard example of agglutinative morphology and postpositional syntax in typological surveys. The Navajo language is the canonical example of polysynthetic verbal morphology. Linguistic relativity shows that typological differences correlate with, though they do not determine, conceptual differences across cultures.
